title: How to Make the First Million Euros
topic: how to make the first million euros
summary: Community advice: index funds and matched retirement saving, ownership over salary, solve painful problems; evidence is US-framed and noisy.
synthesisHtml:
🌐 last30days v3.26.0 · synced 2026-10-14

What I learned:

The boring path is the one people actually describe. In r/AskReddit's "How do you make your first million?" (2026-10-12), the most concrete plan was maxing out employer-matched retirement contributions and buying low-fee S&P 500 index funds. In the "Millionaires of Reddit" thread (2026-09-28, 177 comments), the top replies say it "happened by 4pm market close" inside retirement accounts, and then they went back to work.

Equity and ownership beat salary. The success stories that come up again and again are about owning something: taking stock options instead of a bonus, designing a product, or running an early e-commerce arbitrage. That last one comes with a warning: the commenter said dropshipping was "a wild year" in 2014 and is "dead in 2026". Dan Martell's video (787,789 views) gives the same advice for founders: find a painful problem people will pay to fix ("a painkiller, not a vitamin") and use AI to deliver it cheaply.

You don't always need capital, but commenters push back on that claim. Alex Hormozi's "10 different ways to break down making $1 million" says you can start with little or no money. His top comments push back: "If you're broke, ain't no one lending you that kind of money."

Luck, starting point and leverage matter, and people say so openly. The top Reddit answers joke about being born in a rich country and a "$998k loan from my parents". The "easy, actually" video (796,792 views) points out that leveraged property counts toward net worth: buy a house for 500K, it rises to 1.5M, and net worth goes up by a million. It also warns that ultra-wealth is not the point.

Lots of noise, and almost nothing about Europe. Most of the evidence is US-framed (401k, dollars). The results also picked up off-topic items (a EuroMillions draw, an HN thread on product quality, a GitHub token-cost issue) and "buy my course" pitches. Nothing in this run covers euro-specific routes such as Portuguese or EU tax wrappers. Only 4 of 17 dated items are from the last 7 days.
keyPatterns: Index funds plus employer-matched retirement contributions is the most-cited boring path
Ownership (stock options, products, businesses) shows up in the real success stories
Solve a painful problem people will pay for; AI lowers the cost of delivery
Zero-money-down claims get pushback from commenters
Starting point and leverage (family money, mortgaged property) are openly acknowledged
Evidence is US-framed; no euro or EU-specific guidance in this run
